paragraphs: I believe the State governments would face no real danger from a power in the Union to control them in levying money. I am persuaded that the sense of the people, the extreme risk of provoking the resentment of the State governments, and a conviction that local administrations are useful and necessary for local purposes would together be a complete barrier against any oppressive use of such a power. Even so, I am willing to grant here, in its full extent, the justness of the reasoning which requires that the individual States have an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise their own revenues for their own wants. Having made this concession, I affirm that under the plan of the Convention the States would keep that authority in the most absolute and unqualified sense, with the sole exception of duties on imports and exports. An attempt by the national government to restrict them in using it would be a violent assumption of power, unwarranted by any article or clause of its Constitution.

A complete consolidation of the States into one national sovereignty would mean the complete subordination of the parts, and whatever powers remained in them would depend entirely on the general will. But the plan of the Convention aims only at a partial union or consolidation. The State governments would therefore plainly keep all the rights of sovereignty they had before, except those that were, by that act, EXCLUSIVELY delegated to the United States. This exclusive delegation, or rather this alienation, of State sovereignty would exist in only three cases. The first is where the Constitution in express terms grants an exclusive authority to the Union. The second is where it grants an authority to the Union in one place and prohibits the States from exercising the like authority in another. The third is where it grants the Union an authority to which a similar authority in the States would be absolutely and totally CONTRADICTORY and REPUGNANT. I use these terms to distinguish this last case from another that might look like it but would in fact be essentially different. I mean the case where exercising a concurrent jurisdiction might now and then produce interferences in the POLICY of some branch of administration, but would not imply any direct contradiction or repugnancy in constitutional authority. These three cases of exclusive jurisdiction in the federal government can be illustrated by the following examples. The last clause but one in the eighth section of the first article provides expressly that Congress shall exercise "EXCLUSIVE LEGISLATION" over the district to be appropriated as the seat of government. This answers to the first case. The first clause of the same section empowers Congress "to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts and excises"; and the second clause of the tenth section of the same article declares that "NO STATE SHALL, without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except for the purpose of executing its inspection laws." From these two clauses results an exclusive power in the Union to lay duties on imports and exports, with the one exception mentioned. Another clause, however, which declares that no tax or duty shall be laid on articles exported from any State, narrows this power; with that qualification, it now reaches only the DUTIES ON IMPORTS. This answers to the second case. The third is found in the clause which declares that Congress shall have power "to establish an UNIFORM RULE of naturalization throughout the United States." This must necessarily be exclusive, because if each State had power to prescribe a DISTINCT RULE, there could not be a UNIFORM RULE.

Another case may perhaps be thought to resemble the last, but it is in fact widely different, and it bears directly on the question before us. I mean the power of imposing taxes on all articles other than exports and imports. This, I contend, is plainly a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States. Nothing in the granting clause makes that power EXCLUSIVE in the Union. No separate clause or sentence forbids the States to exercise it. Far from it: a plain and conclusive argument to the contrary can be drawn from the restraint laid on the States regarding duties on imports and exports. That restriction admits that, had it not been inserted, the States would have had the power it excludes. It admits further that, as to all other taxes, the authority of the States remains undiminished. On any other view the restriction would be both unnecessary and dangerous. It would be unnecessary because, if granting the Union the power to lay such duties implied the exclusion of the States, or even their subordination in this particular, no such restriction would be needed. It would be dangerous because introducing it leads directly to the conclusion I have mentioned, which could not have been intended if the objectors' reasoning is right: that in every case the restriction did not cover, the States would have a power of taxation concurrent with the Union's. The restriction in question amounts to what lawyers call a NEGATIVE PREGNANT, that is, a NEGATION of one thing and an AFFIRMANCE of another. It denies the States the authority to impose taxes on imports and exports, and it affirms their authority to impose them on all other articles. It would be mere sophistry to argue that the clause meant to exclude the States ABSOLUTELY from taxes of the former kind and to leave them free to lay others SUBJECT TO THE CONTROL of the national legislature. The restraining or prohibitory clause says only that they shall not, WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF CONGRESS, lay such duties. If we understood this in the sense last mentioned, the Constitution would be made to include a formal provision for the sake of a very absurd conclusion: that the States, WITH THE CONSENT of the national legislature, might tax imports and exports, and might tax every other article UNLESS CONTROLLED by that same body. If this was the intention, why not leave the matter in the first place to what is alleged to be the natural operation of the original clause, which confers a general power of taxation on the Union? Clearly this could not have been the intention, and the clause will not bear such a construction.

A supposed repugnancy between the power of taxation in the States and in the Union cannot be supported in the sense that would be needed to exclude the States. It is certainly possible that a State might tax a particular article in a way that would make it INEXPEDIENT for the Union to lay a further tax on the same article. That would not imply a constitutional inability to impose a further tax. How much to impose, and whether it is expedient to increase the tax on either side, would be questions of prudence for both, and no direct contradiction of power would be involved. The particular policy of the national and State systems of finance might now and then fail to coincide exactly and might require each side to hold back for the other. But it is not a mere possibility of inconvenience in exercising powers; it is an immediate constitutional repugnancy that can, by implication, alienate and extinguish a pre-existing right of sovereignty.

The need for a concurrent jurisdiction in certain cases follows from the division of the sovereign power. The rule that the States keep in full vigor every authority they are not explicitly stripped of in favor of the Union is not a mere theoretical consequence of that division. The whole tenor of the instrument containing the articles of the proposed Constitution clearly admits it. We find there that, although general authorities are granted in the affirmative, the most pointed care was taken, wherever it was thought improper for the States to hold the like authorities, to insert negative clauses forbidding the States to exercise them. The tenth section of the first article consists entirely of such provisions. This is a clear indication of the sense of the Convention, and it furnishes a rule of interpretation drawn from the body of the act itself, which justifies the position I have advanced and refutes every hypothesis to the contrary.
